title: The emotional arcs of stories are dominated by six basic shapes
finding: Classifying sentiment trajectories of 1,327 Project Gutenberg fiction texts with three independent methods, the authors find six core emotional arcs that act as building blocks of more complex trajectories; per authors, particular arcs enjoy greater success as measured by downloads.
why_for_us: Pick one clear emotional shape per episode (and one per season) instead of a flat tone; a 60-90 s episode has room for exactly one fall-and-rise or rise-and-fall.

title: Sentiment Dynamics of Success: Fractal Scaling of Story Arcs Predicts Reader Preferences
finding: For H. C. Andersen's fairy tales, the Hurst exponent of the sentiment arc (its coherence/predictability over time) tracks Goodreads scores: per authors, degrading Hurst values go with degrading scores, and a Hurst exponent between .55 and .65 may be a 'sweet spot' for appreciation.
why_for_us: Emotional beats should be neither random nor fully predictable: keep a coherent emotional line across the 8 episodes but break it with occasional swings.

title: Sentimental Matters - Predicting Literary Quality by Sentiment Analysis and Stylometric Features
venue: Workshop on Computational Approaches to Subjectivity, Sentiment and Social Media Analysis (WASSA)
finding: On a corpus of English-language literary fiction with online user ratings as the target, stylometric features alone help model reader appreciation but, per authors, are outperformed by the novels' sentiment profile (sentiment range and arc patterns). The abstract gives no effect sizes.
why_for_us: How the feeling moves matters more for audience rating than polish of wording; spend script-review time on the emotional range of an episode before line-editing dialogue.

title: Tracing the shapes of adventure: a subject-based interpretation of emotional arcs
finding: Emotional arcs extracted from 1,222 adventure stories from Project Gutenberg again yield six primary modes of emotional change, and per authors the subjects of the stories are often consistent with their emotional mode.
why_for_us: The six-shape result replicates within one genre, so it is safe to use the shapes as a planning grid; match the arc to the episode's topic (e.g. a deadline scare = fall then rise).

title: Happily Ever After: Comparing Sentiment Arcs in Emotionally-Inflected Fanfiction Genres Across Fandoms
venue: Anthology of Computers and the Humanities
finding: Comparing sentiment arcs of Angst, Fluff and Hurt/comfort fanfiction in four fandoms with two sentiment methods, the authors find four arc clusters dominated by particular genres and an 'ending effect': in most stories, regardless of genre, the ending is more positive than the beginning.
why_for_us: Even a tense or gloomy episode should land more positive than it opened; end each episode on relief or a small win at the office before the hook.

title: Success with Style: Using Writing Style to Predict the Success of Novels
venue: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP)
finding: Statistical stylometry discriminates highly successful novels from less successful ones across several genres with accuracy up to 84% per authors; some stylistic characteristics of successful books run contrary to conventional wisdom about good style and readability.
why_for_us: Style carries a measurable success signal independent of plot; fix a consistent voice for narration and dialogue early and keep it across all 8 episodes.

title: Success in books: a big data approach to bestsellers
finding: Analysing New York Times bestsellers and their sales trajectories, the authors report that the higher a book's initial rank, the longer it stays on the list, that fiction authors commonly reach bestseller status with multiple books, and that sales follow a universal pattern whose lifetime total can be predicted from early sales. Per authors, fewer than 500 of over 3 million books published yearly reach the lists.
why_for_us: The launch window decides the trajectory: put the strongest episode and the paid push into the first days, and judge the season from early numbers rather than waiting.

title: Success in books: predicting book sales before publication
finding: Predicting sales before publication with a 'Learning to Place' model, the authors find the publishing house is a strong driver across all genres; for thrillers and mystery the author's previous sales matter most, while in literary fiction and religion the author's visibility plays a more central role.
why_for_us: Distribution and sender reputation outweigh text features; publish through channels notaries already trust (chamber, known practitioners) rather than relying on the script alone.

title: Experimental Study of Inequality and Unpredictability in an Artificial Cultural Market
finding: In an artificial music market with 14,341 participants, showing previous participants' choices increased both inequality and unpredictability of success; per authors, the best songs rarely did poorly and the worst rarely did well, but any other result was possible. The experiment used songs; the authors frame it as explaining hit songs, books and movies.
why_for_us: Quality sets a floor and a ceiling, social proof decides the rest; show early view/share signals with each episode and do not read one episode's result as a verdict on the script.

title: Book Reading Behavior on Goodreads Can Predict the Amazon Best Sellers
venue: IEEE/ACM International Conference on Advances in Social Networks Analysis and Mining (ASONAM)
finding: Features of collective reading behaviour on Goodreads (user posts, genre characteristics) predict whether a book becomes an Amazon best seller with average accuracy of 88.72% using one month of data after publication (85.66% using 15 days) on a balanced set, a 16.4% improvement per authors over a ratings-and-reviews baseline.
why_for_us: Early audience behaviour (comments, shelving, discussion) predicts success better than star ratings; track comments and saves per episode in the first two weeks as the main signal.

title: Using full-text content to characterize and identify best seller books: A study of early 20th-century literature
finding: For books published 1895-1923, classifying Publishers Weekly bestsellers versus non-listed works from full text reached at best an average accuracy of 0.75 (bag-of-words with logistic regression); per authors this underlines how hard it is to predict book success with high accuracy even from the full text.
why_for_us: Text alone leaves roughly a quarter of cases misclassified, so no script formula guarantees a hit; plan for iteration across episodes instead of perfecting episode 1.

title: The Bestseller Code: Anatomy of the Blockbuster Novel
venue: (book; publisher not given in the OpenAlex record)
finding: Book by Archer and Jockers; the OpenAlex record holds only the table of contents, which lists a text-mining 'bestseller-ometer' and chapters on theme, plot ('how to form some perfect curves'), style and character. No results are stated in the record.
why_for_us: Pointer only: a source to read in full for the theme/plot-curve/style/character checklist before fixing the series bible; nothing here should be cited as a finding.

title: The role of transportation in the persuasiveness of public narratives.
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
finding: Transportation (absorption into a story through imagery, affect and attentional focus) increased story-consistent beliefs and favourable evaluations of protagonists (Exp. 1 N=97; replicated in Exp. 3 N=274 and Exp. 4 N=258), and highly transported readers found fewer false notes (Exp. 2 N=69); labelling the story fact or fiction generally made no difference.
why_for_us: Persuasion about the product rides on absorption, not on arguments: keep viewers inside the scene and never break the story for a feature pitch; fictional framing costs nothing.

title: Measuring Narrative Engagement
finding: A scale built on a mental-models approach separates four dimensions of narrative engagement: narrative understanding, attentional focus, emotional engagement and narrative presence; per authors it predicts enjoyment and story-consistent attitudes. It was validated on viewers of film and television in two countries, not on readers.
why_for_us: Use the four dimensions as a per-episode checklist: is it instantly understandable, does it hold attention, does it move, does the office feel present; confusion in the first seconds kills the rest.

title: Defining Identification: A Theoretical Look at the Identification of Audiences With Media Characters
finding: Theoretical article that defines identification with media characters, distinguishes it from other audience reactions to characters and derives hypotheses about its antecedents and consequences; it reports no new data.
why_for_us: Decide per character whether we want identification (the viewer feels as the notary or clerk) or another reaction such as liking; write the lead for identification.

title: The Extended Transportation-Imagery Model: A Meta-Analysis of the Antecedents and Consequences of Consumers' Narrative Transportation
finding: Meta-analysis of 132 effect sizes from 76 published and unpublished articles testing an extended transportation-imagery model with antecedents and consequences of narrative transportation in consumers. The abstract names no individual effect sizes.
why_for_us: The best single source for which story and audience factors raise transportation in a commercial context; read the full antecedent table before locking the format.

title: Identification as a Mechanism of Narrative Persuasion
finding: Two reading experiments (N=120 and N=200) manipulated which of two opposed characters told the story; perspective changed identification and attitudes, and identification mediated the effect of perspective on attitudes.
why_for_us: Whose point of view the episode is told from decides whose side the viewer takes; tell each episode from the notary's or staff member's perspective, never from the software's.

title: Story Perspective and Character Similarity as Drivers of Identification and Narrative Persuasion
finding: In two studies (each N=120, half law students or medical students) readers read about a lawyer or a general practitioner in conflict with another character; both story perspective and the reader's own profession influenced identification, which mediated the effect of perspective on attitude. When readers felt highly similar to the professional's opponent, the mediating effect was blocked.
why_for_us: Direct evidence that professional similarity works for a legal audience: make the protagonist a recognisable notary or notarial clerk, and avoid making a client the more relatable figure in a conflict.

title: A Meta-Analysis Examining the Role of Character-Recipient Similarity in Narrative Persuasion
finding: Across 19 articles and 123 effect sizes, a similar character produced stronger identification (k=34, d=0.14) and self-referencing (k=12, d=0.16), with marginal effects on transportation (d=0.13) and resistance (d=-0.16); per authors, similarity on chosen attributes such as occupation and place of residence had the strongest impact, and the effect intensified with first-person perspective.
why_for_us: Similarity effects are real but small, and occupation is the lever that works best: get the profession details right (deeds, registers, deadlines) rather than matching age or gender.

title: Textual determinants of a component of literary identification
finding: Three experiments on character 'transparency': spelling out information that readers would otherwise infer made a first-person narrator's thoughts and actions harder to understand, and removing free-indirect-speech markers did the same for a third-person central character.
why_for_us: Do not over-explain the character; let viewers infer motives from a look or a half-sentence, which also suits a 60-90 s runtime.

title: Narrative reversals and story success
finding: Measuring narrative reversals as shifts in valence across 30,000 movies, TV shows, novels and fundraising pitches, the authors find that stories with more, and more dramatic, turning points are more successful.
why_for_us: Script at least one clear reversal of fortune into every episode and make it large; a micro-episode with no turn is a sketch, not a story.

title: Affective News: Effects of Discourse Structure in Narratives on Suspense, Curiosity, and Enjoyment While Reading News and Novels
finding: In three studies the same texts were presented in linear, reversal or inverted order and framed as news or novel excerpts: the linear type evoked more suspense, the reversal type more curiosity, and both produced greater reading enjoyment than the inverted type (outcome first), independent of factuality.
why_for_us: Never open with the outcome and then explain; either tell it in order to build suspense or open on a puzzling result and withhold the cause to build curiosity.

title: The psychology of curiosity: A review and reinterpretation.
finding: Review proposing that curiosity is a cognitively induced deprivation arising from the perception of a gap in knowledge or understanding; it also describes curiosity as intense, transient, associated with impulsivity and tending to disappoint when satisfied.
why_for_us: A cliffhanger must open a specific, nameable gap (what was in the envelope?), and the next episode should close it fast and open a new one, because the payoff itself tends to underwhelm.

title: Readers as problem-solvers in the experience of suspense
finding: Seven experiments with texts putting a hero in grave danger: ratings of the likelihood of escape were little affected, but reported suspense was heightened when readers believed the number of paths to a solution had been restricted.
why_for_us: Build suspense by visibly closing off the character's options one by one (system down, client waiting, register closing at 16:00) rather than by raising the stakes.

title: Modelling Suspense in Short Stories as Uncertainty Reduction over Neural Representation
venue: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (ACL)
finding: Comparing surprise (backward-looking) with uncertainty reduction (forward-looking) in a hierarchical language model, evaluated against short stories annotated with human suspense judgements, uncertainty reduction over story representations was the best predictor and reached near human accuracy per authors.
why_for_us: Suspense is about what could still happen, not about what just happened; keep two or three live outcomes open until the last seconds of the episode.

title: Story structure and reader affect in American and Hungarian short stories
venue: University of Illinois technical report (IDEALS repository)
finding: Forty-eight undergraduates read 6 American and 6 Hungarian short stories in five segments, rating suspense, curiosity about the past and future, surprise and irony after each segment and overall liking at the end, as a test of Brewer and Lichtenstein's structural-affect theory on literary texts. The abstract in the record is cut off at 'We found Suspense and Empathy to be the best'.
why_for_us: Suggests suspense and empathy as the two things to protect when cutting an episode for length; treat as a pointer until the full report is read.

title: Story Spoilers Don't Spoil Stories
finding: Three experiments, each with stories from a different genre, tested whether giving away endings in advance impairs enjoyment; the record's abstract sets out the fluency argument that foreknowledge may not ruin pleasure but does not state the results (the title asserts that spoilers do not spoil).
why_for_us: Viewers who know a happy ending is coming (genre promise) can still enjoy the episode; outcome uncertainty is not the only source of pleasure, so recaps and predictable resolutions are affordable.

title: Spoiler Alert: Consequences of Narrative Spoilers for Dimensions of Enjoyment, Appreciation, and Transportation
finding: A within-subjects experiment (N=412) found unspoiled stories more fun and suspenseful and, unexpectedly, also more moving and enjoyable in general; no effect on choice between spoiled and unspoiled stories emerged.
why_for_us: Contradicts the 'spoilers help' result: keep thumbnails, titles and captions from revealing the turn of the episode.

title: The Effect of Spoilers on the Enjoyment of Short Stories
finding: A close replication with different stories found that spoilers presented before a story reduced enjoyment, whereas spoilers presented mid-story had no discernible effect.
why_for_us: Timing matters: protect the reveal before the episode starts (teasers, post copy); a 'previously on' line inside the episode is harmless.

title: On Cliffhangers
finding: Theoretical essay defining the cliffhanger as a misalignment of story and discourse and describing its functions: effects on narrative progression, highlighting continuity and discontinuity, and misleading readers in instrumental ways; it treats cliffhangers as authorial signals for interpretation. No empirical data.
why_for_us: Cut the episode before the scene resolves rather than adding an artificial shock; the place of the cut tells viewers what the series considers important.

title: Wattpad as a resource for literary studies. Quantitative and qualitative examples of the importance of digital social reading and readers' comments in the margins
finding: Mixed-method analysis of stories and margin comments on Wattpad in 13 languages: genre shapes reader behaviour; when reading Teen Fiction, social-bonding (affective interaction, direct emotional response to characters' behaviour) is prevalent, when reading Classics, social-cognitive interaction is prevalent.
why_for_us: Serial readers react to character behaviour moment by moment and bond over it; give each episode one character action worth commenting on and reply in the comments.

title: 웹소설 연재 주기와 연독률의 상관관계 연구 - 웹소설 연재 사이트 문피아 연재작을 중심으로 (Serialization cycle and continued-reading rate of web novels on Munpia)
venue: Studies in Humanities and Social Sciences
finding: Analysis of serials on the Korean web-novel platform Munpia: per author, releasing 7 or more instalments a week helps keep high subscriptions and continued-reading rates; a break in a free serial caused immediate mass reader loss and a sharp fall in views, and in paid serials a break lasting 3 days or more caused mass loss and a drop in continued-reading rate. (Korean-language article, uncited.)
why_for_us: Release cadence is part of the story: publish the 8 episodes on a fixed dense schedule (daily if possible) and never pause mid-season.

title: Analysis of Web Novel Platform Indicators - Focusing on Munpia
venue: The Journal of Humanities and Social Sciences 21
finding: Examining paid purchases, favourites, comments, recommendations and instalment counts of the top 100 works on Munpia: per author, serialization at daily frequency or more is a basic requirement for a hit and for sustaining it, and a sudden rise in comments together with falling recommendations is a warning sign. (Korean-language article.)
why_for_us: Monitor comments against likes per episode: a comment spike with falling likes means viewers are objecting, so adjust the next script before releasing it.

title: What Make a Network Novel Popular? Implications for "Qidian.com"
venue: IEEE International Conference on Big Data (BigData)
finding: Modelling popularity of network novels on Qidian from novel information, reader evaluation and author expertise: number of words and rating positively affect popularity, and per authors rating and number of clicks show a U-shaped relationship. No sample size is given in the abstract.
why_for_us: Volume and accumulated length count on serial platforms; a second season adds to the first's reach, so plan the series as an accumulating catalogue.

title: Modeling Story Expectations: A Generative Framework using LLMs
finding: The authors generate multiple imagined continuations of a story with a language model and extract emotion and narrative-path features from them; in lab survey data and observational data from an online reading platform, these forward-looking expectations are associated with reader engagement above and beyond features of the content already consumed. No effect sizes in the abstract.
why_for_us: What the viewer expects next drives whether they continue; test each episode ending by generating several plausible continuations and keep the ending only if they diverge.

title: Admiration and Frustration: A Multidimensional Analysis of Fanfiction
venue: Computational Humanities Research 2024 (CEUR Workshop Proceedings vol. 3834)
finding: Multidimensional analysis of about 250,000 texts (fanfiction and sources for Lord of the Rings, Harry Potter, Percy Jackson): fan texts do not diverge from their sources in statistically meaningful ways, but fans as a whole prefer stories with less focus on narrative and greater emphasis on character interactions than the source.
why_for_us: The most engaged audience wants more character-to-character interaction and less plot machinery; build episodes around two people in the office talking, not around events.

title: Der Cliffhanger und die serielle Narration: Analyse einer transmedialen Erzähltechnik
finding: Monograph on the cliffhanger, defined as interrupting a serial narrative at a suspenseful moment, tracing it from the Arabian Nights through Victorian and French serial novels, film serials and radio soap operas to TV series, e-books, games and web series; per the abstract it shows a wide variety of forms. No quantitative results.
why_for_us: Background typology of interruption techniques from serial novels that can be mapped to our 8-episode structure; consult for variety so not every episode ends the same way.

title: Reading the Romance: Women, Patriarchy, and Popular Literature.
finding: Based on interviews with forty-two romance readers in a midwestern town, Radway reports that readers find in romances an escape from demanding routines and a hero who supplies tenderness and admiring attention they do not otherwise receive; the heroines they admire are strong, independent and intelligent.
why_for_us: Genre loyalty comes from a need the genre reliably meets; for overworked notarial staff the met need is being competent and appreciated, so let the protagonist be capable and let someone notice it.

title: Adventure, Mystery, and Romance: Formula Stories as Art and Popular Culture
finding: Book by John G. Cawelti on formula stories (adventure, mystery, romance) as art and popular culture; the OpenAlex record has no abstract.
why_for_us: Reference for treating formula as a contract with the audience; to be read before fixing the repeating episode template.

title: The Texas billionaire's pregnant bride: An evolutionary interpretation of romance fiction titles.
venue: Journal of Social, Evolutionary, and Cultural Psychology
finding: Word-frequency and qualitative theme analysis of Harlequin romance titles: per authors the most frequent words and recurring themes are congruent with women's mating interests, which they surmise is the reason for the line's continued international success. No counts are given in the abstract.
why_for_us: Titles work as a promise of the core gratification; name each episode after the concrete thing the audience cares about (the deed, the deadline, the client), not after a product feature.

title: Hierarchy in the Library: Egalitarian Dynamics in Victorian Novels
finding: 519 respondents produced 1,470 protocols on 435 characters from 201 canonical British novels: antagonists are motivated almost exclusively by the desire for social dominance and elicit strongly negative emotional responses, while protagonists are oriented to cooperative and affiliative behaviour and elicit positive responses.
why_for_us: Make the lead a cooperative team player and locate the antagonistic force in someone or something that dominates (an overbearing client, a rigid deadline); do not make the notary a boss who bullies staff.

title: Narrative character networks are associated with storytelling success
finding: Character-interaction networks computed for over 10,000 novels and 1,000 film screenplays: lower clustering is associated with greater novel popularity and higher film ratings, higher modularity is associated only with novel popularity, and shorter path lengths only with film ratings.
why_for_us: Structure the cast so characters connect through a few bridging figures rather than everyone talking to everyone; with 3-4 recurring roles, let one character link the office to the outside.

title: Mystery Appeal: Effects of Uncertainty and Resolution on the Enjoyment of Mystery
finding: In an experiment (N=84) with a manipulated mystery short story, enjoyment during reading was greater when readers were highly uncertain about the culprit and felt high curiosity; a resolution confirming the reader's suspicion was disliked by people with high self-esteem, a surprising resolution by people with low self-esteem.
why_for_us: Keep two candidate explanations alive for any office mystery until the end; neither pure confirmation nor pure surprise pleases everyone, so resolve with a twist that still fits the clues.

title: Murder for Pleasure: Impacts of Plot Complexity and Need for Cognition on Mystery Enjoyment
finding: An experiment with 154 participants reading a four-segment murder story with three levels of clue complexity: higher complexity was generally enjoyed less, and only readers high in need for cognition enjoyed medium complexity most during reading.
why_for_us: Keep the puzzle simple: one clue line per episode; an expert audience tolerates medium complexity at most, and 60-90 s cannot carry more.

title: The Pleasures of Reading Mystery Fiction and Mystery Readers' Book Selection Behavior
venue: Journal of Educational Media & Library Sciences
finding: Grounded-theory study based on in-depth interviews with 21 engaged mystery readers in Taiwan identified reading pleasures including achievement from puzzle solving, amazement at the revelation, satisfied curiosity, compensation from seeing justice, empathy with characters and reflection on social issues; readers select by subgenre, author, series or story.
why_for_us: Small qualitative sample, but a usable list of payoffs to rotate across episodes (solving, revelation, justice done, empathy); 'series' is itself a selection route, so brand the series clearly.

title: Literary quality in the eye of the Dutch reader: The National Reader Survey
finding: A survey of about 14,000 Dutch readers rating novels 1-7 for literary and overall quality found greater agreement than expected; respondents tie literary quality to the text (style, structure, plot, layers) and to genre: a novel seen as a 'genre' novel (suspense, romantic, fantasy) has small chances of a high literary rating.
why_for_us: Audiences rate 'genre' work lower on prestige while still consuming it; do not chase a prestige look, but expect a status-conscious profession to discount soap conventions, so keep the tone dry and exact.
